title: Quantifiers And Witnesses For The Nonclassicality Of Measurements And Of States
authors: Yujie Zhang, Yìlè Yīng, And David Schmid
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2180 (2026).

In recent work [Phys. Rev. X 16, 021050], we proposed a unified notion of nonclassicality that applies to arbitrary processes in quantum theory, including individual quantum states, measurements, and sets thereof. This notion is derived from the principle of generalized noncontextuality, but in a novel manner that applies to individual processes rather than full experiments or theories. In the present work, we develop semidefinite-programming-based certificates and witnesses for the nonclassicality of states, sources, measurements, and sets thereof. These theory-dependent methods complement theory-independent approaches based on noncontextuality inequalities. We demonstrate the framework through a variety of explicit examples.

.
tldr: This paper develops semidefinite-programming-based certificates and witnesses for the nonclassicality of quantum states, measurements, and sets thereof, based on generalized noncontextuality.
motivation: To provide practical tools for detecting and quantifying nonclassicality in quantum processes, complementing theory-independent noncontextuality inequalities.
method: The authors formulate semidefinite programs that serve as certificates and witnesses for nonclassicality, applicable to individual states, measurements, and sets, and demonstrate them with examples.
result: They present explicit SDP-based methods that can certify nonclassicality in various scenarios, as illustrated through examples.
conclusion: The work offers a versatile framework for nonclassicality detection, advancing the study of quantum contextuality and its applications.

title: Stabilizer Ranks, Barnes Wall Lattices And Magic Monotones
authors: Amolak Ratan Kalra And Pulkit Sinha
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2179 (2026).

In 2024, Kliuchnikov and Schönnenbeck showed a connection between the Barnes Wall lattices, stabilizer states and Clifford operations. In this work, we study their results and relate them to the problem of lower bounding stabilizer ranks. We show the first quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity as a function of stabilizer ranks, which reproduces the linear-by-log lower bound for [MATH], i.e, on the approximate stabilizer rank of [MATH]. In fact, we show that the lower bound holds even when the fidelity between the approximation and [MATH] is exponentially small, which is currently the best lower bound in this regime. Next, we define a new magic monotone for pure states, the Barnes Wall norm, and its corresponding approximate variant. We upper bound these monotones by the [MATH]-count of state preparation, and also by the stabilizer ranks. In particular, the upper bound given by the [MATH]-count is tight, in the sense that we exhibit states that achieve the bound. Apart from these results, we give a Fidelity Amplification algorithm, which provides a trade-off between approximation error and the stabilizer rank. As a corollary, it gives us a way to compose approximate stabilizer decompositions into approximate decompositions of their tensor products. Finally, we provide an alternate, elementary proof of the existence and density of product states with maximal stabilizer ranks, which was first proven by Lovitz and Steffan (2022), where they used results from algebraic geometry.

.
tldr: This paper connects Barnes Wall lattices to stabilizer ranks, providing new lower bounds and a magic monotone.
motivation: To understand and improve bounds on stabilizer ranks, which are crucial for quantum resource theories and magic state distillation.
method: The authors study the connection between Barnes Wall lattices and stabilizer states, derive quantitative lower bounds on stabilizer fidelity, define a new magic monotone (Barnes Wall norm), and provide a fidelity amplification algorithm.
result: They obtain the best lower bound on approximate stabilizer rank for magic states, show tight upper bounds for the new monotone, and give an elementary proof of existence of product states with maximal stabilizer ranks.
conclusion: The work advances the resource theory of magic states by providing new tools and bounds, with implications for quantum computation and information.

title: A Complete Theory Of The Clifford Commutant
authors: Lennart Bittel, Jens Eisert, Lorenzo Leone, Antonio A. Mele, And Salvatore F.E. Oliviero
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2171 (2026).

The Clifford group plays a central role in quantum information science. It is the building block for many error-correcting schemes and matches the first three moments of the Haar measure over the unitary group-a property that is essential for a broad range of quantum algorithms, with applications in pseudorandomness, learning theory, benchmarking, and entanglement distillation. At the heart of understanding many properties of the Clifford group lies the Clifford commutant: the set of operators that commute with [MATH]-fold tensor powers of Clifford unitaries. Previous understanding of this commutant has been limited to relatively small values of [MATH], constrained by the number of qubits [MATH]. In this work, we develop a complete theory of the Clifford commutant. Our first result provides an explicit orthogonal basis for the commutant and computes its dimension for arbitrary [MATH] and [MATH]. We also introduce an alternative and easy-to-manipulate basis formed by isotropic sums of Pauli operators. We show that this basis is generated by products of permutations, which generate the unitary group commutant, and at most three other operators. Additionally, we develop a graphical calculus allowing a diagrammatic manipulation of elements of this basis. These results enable a wealth of applications: among others, we characterize all measurable magic measures and identify optimal strategies for stabilizer property testing, whose success probability also offers an operational interpretation to stabilizer entropies. Finally, we show that these results also generalize to multi-qudit systems with prime local dimension.

.
tldr: This paper provides a complete theory of the Clifford commutant, offering explicit bases and a graphical calculus, with applications to magic measures and stabilizer property testing.
motivation: The Clifford group is central to quantum information, but the structure of its commutant was only partially understood for small tensor powers and qubit numbers. A complete theory is needed to unlock applications in pseudorandomness, learning, and entanglement distillation.
method: The authors derive an explicit orthogonal basis for the Clifford commutant for arbitrary tensor power and qubit number, introduce an alternative basis of isotropic sums of Pauli operators, and develop a graphical calculus for manipulating these basis elements.
result: They compute the dimension of the commutant, show the basis is generated by permutations and at most three other operators, and apply the theory to characterize all measurable magic measures and identify optimal strategies for stabilizer property testing, with an operational interpretation of stabilizer entropies.
conclusion: The complete theory of the Clifford commutant provides a powerful tool for quantum information, with implications for magic resource theory and property testing, and extends to multi-qudit systems with prime local dimension.

title: Fast Quantum Measurement Tomography With Optimal Error Bounds
authors: Leonardo Zambrano, Sergi Ramos-Calderer, And Richard Kueng
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2162 (2026).

We present a two-step protocol for quantum measurement tomography that is light on classical co-processing cost and still achieves optimal sample complexity. Given measurement data from a known probe state ensemble, we first apply least-squares estimation to produce an unconstrained approximation of the POVM, and then project this estimate onto the set of valid quantum measurements. For a POVM with [MATH] outcomes acting on a [MATH]-dimensional system, we show that the protocol requires [MATH] samples to achieve error [MATH] in worst-case distance, and [MATH] samples in average-case distance. We further establish two matching sample complexity lower bounds of [MATH] and [MATH] for any non-adaptive, single-copy POVM tomography protocol. Hence, our projected least squares POVM tomography is sample-optimal in both the dimension and the number of outcomes for both distances. Our method admits an analytic form when using global or local 2-designs as probe ensembles and enables rigorous non-asymptotic error guarantees. Finally, we also complement our findings with empirical performance studies carried out on a noisy superconducting quantum computer with flux-tunable transmon qubits.

.
tldr: This paper presents a sample-optimal two-step protocol for quantum measurement tomography using projected least squares, with rigorous error bounds and experimental validation on a superconducting quantum computer.
motivation: Quantum measurement tomography is essential for characterizing quantum devices, but existing protocols often have high classical processing cost or suboptimal sample complexity. The authors aim to design a protocol that is both computationally efficient and sample-optimal.
method: The protocol first applies least-squares estimation to measurement data from known probe states, then projects the unconstrained estimate onto the set of valid POVMs. They analyze sample complexity for worst-case and average-case distances, and establish matching lower bounds for any non-adaptive single-copy protocol.
result: The protocol achieves optimal sample complexity in both dimension and number of outcomes for both distances, with analytic forms for global and local 2-designs. Empirical tests on a noisy superconducting quantum computer confirm its practical effectiveness.
conclusion: The proposed projected least squares method provides a sample-optimal and computationally light solution for quantum measurement tomography, with strong theoretical guarantees and practical viability.

title: Towards Unconditional Uncloneable Encryption
authors: Pierre Botteron, Anne Broadbent, Eric Culf, Ion Nechita, Clément Pellegrini, And Denis Rochette
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2157 (2026).

Uncloneable encryption is a cryptographic primitive which encrypts a classical message into a quantum ciphertext, such that two quantum adversaries are limited in their capacity of being able to simultaneously decrypt, given the key and quantum side-information produced from the ciphertext. Since its initial proposal and scheme in the random oracle model by Broadbent and Lord [TQC 2020], uncloneable encryption has developed into an important primitive at the foundation of quantum uncloneability for cryptographic primitives. Despite sustained efforts, however, the question of unconditional uncloneable encryption (and in particular of the simplest case, called an uncloneable bit) has remained elusive. Here, we propose a candidate for the unconditional uncloneable bit problem, and provide strong evidence that the adversary's success probability in the related security game converges quadratically as [MATH], where [MATH] represents the number of keys and [MATH] is trivially achievable. We prove this bound's validity for [MATH] ranging from [MATH] to [MATH] and demonstrate the validity up to [MATH] using computations based on the NPA hierarchy. We furthemore provide compelling heuristic evidence towards the general case. In addition, we prove an asymptotic upper bound of [MATH] and give a numerical upper bound of [MATH], which to our knowledge is the best-known value in the unconditional model.

.
tldr: This paper proposes a candidate for unconditional uncloneable encryption and provides strong evidence for its security, with quadratic convergence of adversary success probability.
motivation: Uncloneable encryption is a fundamental primitive in quantum cryptography, but unconditional security (without random oracles) has remained elusive. The authors aim to resolve this open problem.
method: They propose a specific scheme for an uncloneable bit and analyze its security using the NPA hierarchy and other techniques, proving bounds for certain parameter ranges and providing numerical evidence.
result: They prove the adversary's success probability converges quadratically for a range of key numbers, and provide an asymptotic upper bound and a numerical upper bound that is the best known.
conclusion: The work provides strong evidence for the feasibility of unconditional uncloneable encryption, advancing the theoretical foundations of quantum cryptography.

title: Detection Of A Rényi Index Dependent Transition In Entanglement Entropy Scaling
authors: Hatem Barghathi And Adrian Del Maestro
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2184 (2026).

The scaling of entanglement with subsystem size encodes key information about phases and criticality, but the von Neumann entropy is costly to access in experiments and simulations, often requiring full state tomography. The second Rényi entropy is readily measured using two-copy protocols and is often used as a proxy for the von Neumann entanglement entropy, where it is assumed to track its asymptotic scaling. Sugino and Korepiny (Int. J. Mod. Phys. B 32, 1850306 (2018)) revealed that in the ground state of some highly constrained spin models, the scaling of the von Neumann and Rényi entropies can differ, varying from power law to logarithmic scaling as a function of the Rényi index. Here, we construct a number-conserving many-body state that demonstrates a Rényi-index-dependent change in the leading entanglement scaling, generalizing previous results to the case of interacting fermions. We introduce a symmetry-aware lower bound on the von Neumann entropy built from charge-resolved Rényi entropies that can provide a protocol for diagnosing anomalous entanglement scaling from experimentally accessible data.

.
tldr: This paper constructs a number-conserving fermionic state exhibiting a Rényi-index-dependent transition in entanglement entropy scaling and introduces a symmetry-aware lower bound on von Neumann entropy from charge-resolved Rényi entropies.
motivation: The von Neumann entropy is difficult to measure experimentally, so the second Rényi entropy is often used as a proxy. However, in some constrained spin models, the scaling of these entropies can differ, and this work aims to generalize this phenomenon to interacting fermions and provide a diagnostic protocol.
method: The authors construct a number-conserving many-body state that demonstrates a Rényi-index-dependent change in leading entanglement scaling. They also introduce a symmetry-aware lower bound on the von Neumann entropy built from charge-resolved Rényi entropies.
result: The constructed state shows a transition from power-law to logarithmic scaling of entanglement entropy as a function of the Rényi index, generalizing previous results to interacting fermions. The proposed lower bound can diagnose anomalous entanglement scaling from experimentally accessible data.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework and experimental protocol for detecting Rényi-index-dependent entanglement scaling, which is relevant for understanding phases and criticality in quantum systems.

title: Quantum Nonlocality Without Entanglement And State Discrimination Measures
authors: Shayeef Murshid, Tathagata Gupta, Vincent Russo, And Somshubhro Bandyopadhyay
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2174 (2026).

An ensemble of product states is said to exhibit “quantum nonlocality without entanglement” if it cannot be optimally discriminated using local operations and classical communication (LOCC). We show that this property can depend on the chosen discrimination measure. Specifically, we construct a family of ensembles, each consisting of six linearly independent, equally probable bipartite product states, for which LOCC fails to achieve optimal minimum-error discrimination but succeeds in achieving optimal unambiguous discrimination. We further extend our construction to multipartite systems and provide strong numerical evidence that a similar separation between local and global optima is present for minimum-error discrimination, but not for unambiguous discrimination.

.
tldr: This paper shows that quantum nonlocality without entanglement can depend on the discrimination measure, constructing ensembles where LOCC fails for minimum-error but succeeds for unambiguous discrimination.
motivation: To understand how the choice of discrimination measure affects the phenomenon of quantum nonlocality without entanglement, which is fundamental to quantum information processing.
method: The authors construct explicit ensembles of six linearly independent, equally probable bipartite product states and analyze their optimal discrimination under LOCC for both minimum-error and unambiguous discrimination, extending to multipartite systems with numerical evidence.
result: They find a separation: LOCC cannot achieve optimal minimum-error discrimination but can achieve optimal unambiguous discrimination for the constructed ensembles, with similar separation observed numerically in multipartite cases.
conclusion: The property of quantum nonlocality without entanglement is measure-dependent, highlighting the importance of specifying the discrimination task when studying such phenomena.

title: Non-commutative Optimization Problems With Differential Constraints
authors: Mateus Araújo, Andrew J. P. Garner, And Miguel Navascues
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2169 (2026).

Non-commutative polynomial optimization (NPO) problems seek to minimize the state average of a polynomial of some operator variables, subject to polynomial constraints, over all states and operators, as well as the Hilbert spaces where those might be defined. Many of these problems are known to admit a complete hierarchy of semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations. In this work, we consider a variant of NPO problems where a subset of the operator variables satisfies a system of ordinary differential equations. We prove that, under mild conditions of operator boundedness, for every such problem one can construct a standard NPO problem with the same solution. This allows us to define a complete hierarchy of SDPs to tackle the original differential problem. We apply this method to bound averages of local observables in quantum spin systems subject to a Hamiltonian evolution (i.e., a quench). We find that, even in the thermodynamic limit of infinitely many sites, low levels of the hierarchy provide very good approximations for reasonably long evolution times.

.
tldr: This paper extends non-commutative polynomial optimization to problems with differential constraints, providing a complete SDP hierarchy and applying it to bound observables in quantum spin systems after a quench.
motivation: Many quantum information problems involve operator variables that evolve under differential equations, which are not directly handled by standard NPO. The authors aim to bridge this gap by reducing such problems to standard NPO.
method: They prove that under boundedness conditions, any NPO with differential constraints can be transformed into an equivalent standard NPO, enabling the use of existing SDP hierarchies. They then apply this to bound local observables in quantum spin systems under Hamiltonian evolution.
result: The method yields a complete SDP hierarchy, and low levels provide good approximations for reasonably long evolution times even in the thermodynamic limit.
conclusion: This work provides a new tool for analyzing quantum dynamics with optimization techniques, potentially useful for quantum information and many-body physics.

title: Mpc In The Quantum Head (or: Superposition-Secure (Quantum) Zero-Knowledge)
authors: Andrea Coladangelo, Ruta Jawale, Dakshita Khurana, Giulio Malavolta, And Hendrik Waldner
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2161 (2026).

The MPC-in-the-head technique (Ishai et al., STOC 2007) is a celebrated method to build zero-knowledge protocols with desirable theoretical properties and high practical efficiency. This technique has generated a large body of research and has influenced the design of real-world post-quantum cryptographic signatures. In this work, we present a generalization of the MPC-in-the-head paradigm to the quantum setting, where the MPC is running a quantum computation. As an application of our framework, we propose a new approach to build zero-knowledge protocols where security holds even against a verifier that can obtain a superposition of transcripts. This notion was pioneered by Damgard et al., who built a zero-knowledge protocol for NP (in the common reference string model) secure against superposition attacks, by relying on perfectly hiding and unconditionally binding dual-mode commitments. Unfortunately, no such commitments are known from standard cryptographic assumptions. In this work we revisit this problem, and present two new three-round protocols in the common reference string model: (i) A zero-knowledge argument for NP, whose security reduces to the standard learning with errors (LWE) problem. (ii) A zero-knowledge argument for QMA from the same assumption.

.
tldr: This paper generalizes the MPC-in-the-head technique to the quantum setting, yielding zero-knowledge protocols secure against superposition attacks from standard LWE assumptions.
motivation: Existing zero-knowledge protocols secure against superposition attacks rely on dual-mode commitments not known from standard assumptions. The authors aim to construct such protocols from standard LWE.
method: They introduce a quantum generalization of MPC-in-the-head, where the MPC runs a quantum computation, and use it to build three-round zero-knowledge arguments for NP and QMA in the common reference string model.
result: They obtain two new three-round protocols: one for NP and one for QMA, both secure against superposition attacks and based on the LWE assumption.
conclusion: This work provides a new framework for quantum zero-knowledge with practical implications for post-quantum cryptography, advancing the field of quantum information and cryptography.

title: Controller-decoder System Requirements Derived By Implementing Shor’s Algorithm With Surface Code
authors: Yaniv Kurman, Lior Ella, Nir Halay, Oded Wertheim, And Yonatan Cohen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2170 (2026).

Quantum Error Correction (QEC) is regarded as the most promising path to quantum advantage. The success of QEC relies on achieving quantum gate fidelities below the error threshold of the QEC code, while accurately decoding errors through classical processing of the QEC stabilizer measurements. In this paper, we uncover the critical system-level requirements from a controller-decoder system (CDS) necessary to successfully execute the next milestone in QEC: a non-Clifford circuit. Using a representative non-Clifford circuit, of Shor factorization algorithm for the number 21, we convert the logical-level circuit to a QEC surface code circuit and finally to the physical level circuit. By taking into account realistic implementation aspects using typical superconducting qubit processor parameters, we reveal a broad range of core requirements from any CDS aimed at performing error corrected quantum computation. Our findings indicate that the controller-decoder closed-loop latency must remain within tens of microseconds, achievable by distributing decoding data into several decoders while ensuring fast communication between decoders and with the controller. By extending existing simulation techniques, we simulate the complete fault-tolerant factorization circuit at the physical level, demonstrating that near-term hardware performance in the scale of 0.1% physical error rates and 1000 qubits, are sufficient for a successful circuit execution. Overall, the requirements outlined here set the stage for near- and medium-term experimental realizations of non-Clifford QEC circuits.

A video of the physical-level gate sequences for the factorization circuit with distance-3 surfaces. (doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17970554)

.
tldr: This paper derives system-level requirements for a controller-decoder system to execute non-Clifford circuits with surface code QEC, using Shor's algorithm for 21 as a case study.
motivation: The next milestone in quantum error correction is executing non-Clifford circuits, which requires understanding the system-level demands on classical control and decoding.
method: The authors convert a logical-level Shor circuit to a surface code circuit and then to a physical-level circuit, simulating the full fault-tolerant factorization with realistic superconducting qubit parameters.
result: They find that controller-decoder latency must be within tens of microseconds, achievable with distributed decoders, and that near-term hardware with ~0.1% error rates and ~1000 qubits suffices.
conclusion: The outlined requirements provide a roadmap for near-term experimental realization of non-Clifford QEC circuits.

title: Modulator-Assisted Zeno Control Of Energy Transfer In Quantum Batteries
authors: Songbo Xie, Manas Sajjan, Ashok Ajoy, And Sabre Kais
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2178 (2026).

Efficient operation of quantum batteries requires not only fast energy transfer but also the ability to halt the charging process to prevent reverse flow. Existing approaches typically rely on direct control of the charger-battery interaction, which can be experimentally demanding. Here we propose a modulator-assisted quantum battery protocol that enables indirect control of energy transfer while keeping the interaction always on. By applying repeated local unitary operations to an auxiliary modulator qubit, we exploit a Zeno-like mechanism to dynamically reshape the effective Hamiltonian and switch the charger-battery coupling on and off. We demonstrate this mechanism in a minimal three-body model and show that it remains effective beyond the ideal fast-control limit. We further extend the protocol to a collective many-body architecture, where it preserves the characteristic enhancement of charging power, scaling as [MATH] with the number of battery units. We also discuss a possible implementation in an NV-[MATH]C spin platform. Our results establish modulator-assisted Zeno control as a scalable route to regulating energy transfer in quantum batteries.

.
tldr: This paper proposes a modulator-assisted Zeno control protocol for quantum batteries, enabling indirect control of energy transfer while keeping the charger-battery interaction always on.
motivation: Efficient quantum battery operation requires halting charging to prevent reverse flow, but direct control of the interaction is experimentally demanding. The authors aim to achieve indirect control via a modulator qubit.
method: They apply repeated local unitary operations to an auxiliary modulator qubit, exploiting a Zeno-like mechanism to dynamically reshape the effective Hamiltonian and switch the charger-battery coupling on and off. They demonstrate this in a minimal three-body model and extend to a collective many-body architecture.
result: The protocol works beyond the ideal fast-control limit, preserves the collective charging power enhancement scaling with the number of battery units, and is feasible in an NV-13C spin platform.
conclusion: Modulator-assisted Zeno control offers a scalable route to regulating energy transfer in quantum batteries, addressing a key challenge in quantum thermodynamics.

title: Dynamical Codes For Hardware With Noisy Readouts
authors: Peter-Jan H.S. Derks, Alex Townsend-Teague, Jens Eisert, Markus S. Kesselring, Oscar Higgott, And Benjamin J. Brown
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2176 (2026).

Dynamical stabilizer codes may offer a practical route to large-scale quantum computation. Such codes are defined by a schedule of error-detecting measurements, which allows for flexibility in their construction. In this work, we ask how best to optimise the measurement schedule of dynamically condensed colour codes in various limits of noise bias. We take a particular focus on the setting where measurements introduce more noise than unitary and idling operations – a noise model relevant to some hardware proposals. For measurement-biased noise models, we improve code performance by strategically repeating measurements within the schedule. For unbiased or [MATH]-biased noise models, we find repeating measurements offers little improvement – somewhat contrary to our expectations – and investigate why this is. To perform this analysis, we generalise a metric called the teraquop footprint to the teraquop volume. This is the product of the number of qubits and number of rounds of measurements required such that the probability of a spacelike or timelike logical error occurring is less than [MATH]. In most cases, we find differences in performance are primarily due to the number of rounds of measurements required, rather than the number of qubits – emphasising the importance of using the teraquop volume in the analysis. Additionally, our results provide another example of the importance of making use of correlated errors when decoding, in that using belief matching rather than minimum-weight perfect matching can turn a worst-performing code under a given noise model into a best-performing code.

.
tldr: This paper optimizes measurement schedules for dynamical color codes under measurement-biased noise, introducing the teraquop volume metric and showing that belief matching decoding can significantly improve performance.
motivation: Dynamical stabilizer codes may enable large-scale quantum computation, but their performance under realistic noise models, especially measurement-biased noise, is not well understood. The authors aim to optimize measurement schedules to improve error correction.
method: They analyze dynamically condensed color codes under various noise biases, using the teraquop volume (product of qubits and measurement rounds) as a metric. They compare decoding strategies, specifically belief matching versus minimum-weight perfect matching.
result: Repeating measurements improves performance under measurement-biased noise, but offers little benefit for unbiased or X-biased noise. The teraquop volume reveals that differences are mainly due to measurement rounds, not qubit count. Belief matching can turn a worst-performing code into a best-performing one.
conclusion: The study provides practical guidance for optimizing dynamical codes in hardware with noisy readouts, emphasizing the importance of measurement scheduling and advanced decoding techniques.

title: A Partition Function Framework For Estimating Logical Error Curves In Stabilizer Codes
authors: Leon Wichette, Hans Hohenfeld, Elie Mounzer, And Linnea Grans-Samuelsson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2175 (2026).

Based on the mapping between stabilizer quantum error correcting codes and disordered statistical mechanics models, we define a ratio of partition functions that measures the success probability for maximum partition function decoding, which at the Nishimori temperature corresponds to maximum likelihood (ML) decoding. We show that this ratio differs from the similarly defined order probability and describe the decoding strategy whose success rate is described by the order probability. We refer to the latter as a probabilistic partition function decoding and show that it is the strategy that at zero temperature corresponds to maximum probability (MP) decoding. Based on the difference between the two decoders, we discuss the possibility of a maximum partition function decodability boundary outside the order-disorder phase boundary. At zero temperature, the difference between the two ratios measures to what degree MP decoding can be improved by accounting for degeneracy among maximum probability errors, through methods such as ensembling. We consider in detail the example of the toric code under bitflip noise, which maps to the Random Bond Ising Model. We demonstrate that estimation of logical performance through decoding probability and order probability is more sample efficient than estimation by counting failures of the corresponding decoders, especially in the regime of low noise. We consider both uniform noise and noise where qubits are given individual error rates. The latter noise model lifts the degeneracy among maximum probability errors, but we show that ensembling remains useful as long as it also samples less probable errors. We also consider, in less detail, the color code under bitflip and depolarizing noise.

.
tldr: This paper introduces a partition function framework to estimate logical error rates in stabilizer codes, connecting decoding success to statistical mechanics and demonstrating improved sample efficiency.
motivation: Accurate estimation of logical error rates is crucial for assessing quantum error correction performance, but direct simulation of decoders can be inefficient, especially at low noise rates.
method: The authors define a ratio of partition functions corresponding to maximum partition function decoding (ML at Nishimori temperature) and compare it to order probability for probabilistic decoding (MP at zero temperature). They analyze the toric code under bitflip noise via the Random Bond Ising Model and also consider color codes.
result: They show that the partition function ratio differs from order probability, and that estimating decoding probability and order probability is more sample-efficient than counting decoder failures, particularly at low noise. They also discuss the impact of degeneracy and individual error rates.
conclusion: The proposed framework provides a more efficient method for estimating logical error curves and offers insights into decoding strategies and potential decodability boundaries.

title: Hoare Meets Heisenberg: A Lightweight Logic For Quantum Programs
authors: Aarthi Sundaram, Robert Rand, Kartik Singhal, Youngchan Cho, And Brad Lackey
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2172 (2026).

We show that Gottesman's (1998) semantics for Clifford circuits based on the Heisenberg representation gives rise to a lightweight Hoare-like logic for efficiently characterizing a common subset of quantum programs. Our applications include (i) certifying whether auxiliary qubits can be safely disposed of, (ii) determining if a system is separable across a given bipartition, (iii) checking the transversality of a gate with respect to a given stabilizer code, and (iv) computing post-measurement states for computational basis measurements. Further, this logic is extended to accommodate universal quantum computing by deriving Hoare triples for the [MATH]-gate, multiply-controlled unitaries such as the Toffoli gate, and some gate injection circuits that use associated magic states. A number of interesting results emerge from this logic, including a lower bound on the number of [MATH] gates necessary to perform a multiply-controlled [MATH] gate.

.
tldr: This paper introduces a lightweight Hoare-like logic for quantum programs based on Gottesman's Heisenberg representation, enabling efficient reasoning about Clifford circuits and extensions to universal quantum computing.
motivation: To provide a practical and efficient method for reasoning about quantum programs, particularly for certification tasks like qubit disposal, separability, and gate transversality, which are important for quantum error correction and fault tolerance.
method: The authors formalize a Hoare logic using the Heisenberg representation of Clifford circuits, deriving Hoare triples for Clifford operations and extending to non-Clifford gates like T-gates and Toffoli via gate injection and magic states.
result: The logic enables efficient certification of auxiliary qubit disposal, bipartite separability, gate transversality, and post-measurement states. It also yields a lower bound on the number of T-gates needed for multiply-controlled gates.
conclusion: The proposed logic provides a lightweight and useful tool for reasoning about quantum programs, with applications in quantum error correction and fault-tolerant quantum computing, though it is not a primary focus of the user's interests.

title: Optimal Schedule Of Multi-channel Quantum Zeno Dragging With Application To Solving The k-SAT Problem
authors: Yipei Zhang, Alain Sarlette, Philippe Lewalle, Tathagata Karmakar, Thilo Scharnhorst, And K. Birgitta Whaley
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2167 (2026).

Quantum Zeno dragging enables the preparation of common eigenstates of a set of observables by frequent measurement and adiabatic-like modulation of the measurement basis. In this work, we present a deeper analysis of multi-channel Zeno dragging using generalized measurements, i.e. simultaneously measuring a set of non-commuting observables that vary slowly in time, to drag the state towards a target subspace. For concreteness, we will focus on a measurement-driven approach to solving k-SAT problems as examples. We first compute some analytical upper bounds on the convergence time, including the effect of finite measurement time resolution. We then apply optimal control theory to obtain the optimal dragging schedule that lower bounds the convergence time, for low-dimensional settings. This study provides a theoretical foundation for multi-channel Zeno dragging and its optimization, and also serves as a guide for designing optimal dragging schedules for quantum information tasks including measurement-driven quantum algorithms.

.
tldr: This paper analyzes multi-channel quantum Zeno dragging with generalized measurements and applies optimal control to find schedules that minimize convergence time, with applications to solving k-SAT problems.
motivation: Quantum Zeno dragging can prepare target states via frequent measurements, but multi-channel versions with non-commuting observables lack rigorous analysis and optimization. The authors aim to provide theoretical foundations and optimal schedules for such protocols.
method: The authors derive analytical upper bounds on convergence time, including finite measurement resolution effects, and use optimal control theory to find schedules that lower-bound convergence time in low-dimensional settings.
result: They obtain analytical bounds and optimal dragging schedules that improve convergence time, demonstrated on k-SAT problem instances.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical foundation for multi-channel Zeno dragging and offers guidance for designing optimal schedules for measurement-driven quantum algorithms.

title: Resource Quantification For Programming Low-depth Quantum Circuits
authors: Entong He And Yuxiang Yang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2166 (2026).

Noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices pave the way for implementing quantum algorithms that offer quantum advantages over their classical counterparts. Due to the intrinsic noise and decoherence in the physical system, NISQ machines are naturally modeled as large-scale, low-depth quantum circuits. In practice, executing such circuits requires sending program states that encode the relevant instructions to a programmable quantum computer, typically through a cloud service. Existing programming approaches designed for generic unitary transformations are computationally inefficient in the low-depth setting, and therefore remain unsatisfactory. As such, to realize NISQ algorithms, it is crucial to find an efficient way to program low-depth circuits as the number of qubits [MATH] increases. Here, we investigate the circuit complexity and the size of quantum memory, known as the program cost, required to program low-depth brickwork circuits. We establish a tight worst-case program cost of [MATH] for universally programming low-depth brickwork circuits in the large-[MATH] regime. Moreover, we analyze the trade-off between the cost of describing the layout of local gates and the cost of programming them to implement the target unitaries via the light-cone argument. Our findings suggest that faithful gate-wise programming is essentially optimal in the low-depth regime.

.
tldr: This paper establishes tight bounds on the program cost (quantum memory size) required to universally program low-depth brickwork circuits, showing that gate-wise programming is essentially optimal in the low-depth regime.
motivation: Programming NISQ devices efficiently is crucial, but existing methods for generic unitary transformations are inefficient for low-depth circuits. The authors aim to find an efficient way to program low-depth circuits as the number of qubits grows.
method: The authors analyze the circuit complexity and quantum memory size (program cost) needed to program low-depth brickwork circuits. They use the light-cone argument to study the trade-off between describing the layout of local gates and programming them.
result: They establish a tight worst-case program cost for universally programming low-depth brickwork circuits in the large-qubit regime, and show that faithful gate-wise programming is essentially optimal.
conclusion: The findings provide a fundamental limit on the resources needed to program low-depth quantum circuits, which is important for practical NISQ computing.

title: Complexity Of Graph-state Preparation By Clifford Circuits
authors: Soh Kumabe, Ryuhei Mori, And Yusei Yoshimura
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2165 (2026).

In this work, we study the complexity of graph-state preparation in a general model of quantum algorithms that allows measurements in the computational basis, single-qubit Clifford operations, and two-qubit Clifford operations. We define the CZ-complexity of a graph state [MATH] as the minimum number of two-qubit Clifford operations required to generate [MATH] from [MATH] for some [MATH]. Equivalently, every optimal algorithm can be taken to use only controlled-Z (CZ) gates as its two-qubit Clifford operations. We then give a combinatorial characterization of graph-state transformations. Specifically, [MATH] can be generated from another graph state [MATH] by an algorithm of CZ-complexity at most [MATH] if and only if [MATH] can be obtained from [MATH] by vertex deletions, local complementations and at most [MATH] elementary edge-complementations. Here, an elementary edge-complementation toggles either a single edge, all edges between one vertex and the neighborhood of another, or all edges between the neighborhoods of two non-adjacent vertices. Using this characterization, we relate CZ-complexity to rank-width. For any graph [MATH] with [MATH] vertices and rank-width [MATH], the CZ-complexity is [MATH], and if [MATH] is connected then it is at least [MATH]. We also show that these bounds are close to optimal. Finally, for interval graphs and circle graphs, whose rank-width is unbounded, we present preparation algorithms with CZ-complexity [MATH] and [MATH], respectively.

.
tldr: This paper characterizes the minimum number of two-qubit Clifford operations (CZ-complexity) needed to prepare graph states, linking it to graph transformations and rank-width.
motivation: Understanding the resource cost of preparing graph states is crucial for quantum information processing, as graph states are key resources for measurement-based quantum computing and quantum error correction.
method: The authors define CZ-complexity and prove a combinatorial characterization of graph-state transformations using vertex deletions, local complementations, and elementary edge-complementations. They then relate CZ-complexity to rank-width and provide algorithms for interval and circle graphs.
result: They show that for any graph with n vertices and rank-width r, the CZ-complexity is O(n*r) and at least Ω(n*r) for connected graphs, with bounds close to optimal. They also give O(n) and O(n log n) algorithms for interval and circle graphs, respectively.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous framework for quantifying the complexity of graph-state preparation, offering both theoretical bounds and practical algorithms, which is valuable for optimizing quantum resource usage.

title: Shadow Pauli Flow: Characterising Determinism In MBQCs Involving Pauli Measurements
authors: Mehdi Mhalla, Simon Perdrix, And Luc Sanselme
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2163 (2026).

We introduce a new characterisation of determinism in Measurement-Based Quantum Computing (MBQC). The one-way model consists in performing local measurements over a large entangled state represented by a graph. The ability to perform an overall deterministic computation requires a correction strategy because of the non-determinism of each measurement. The existence of such a correction strategy depends on the underlying open graph, which is a description of the resource state together with the basis of the performed measurements. GFlow is a well-known graphical characterisation of robust determinism in MBQC when every measurement is performed in some specific planes of the Bloch sphere. While Pauli measurements are ubiquitous in MBQC, GFlow fails to be necessary for determinism when a measurement-based quantum computation involves Pauli measurements. Pauli Flow was designed as a generalisation of GFlow to handle MBQC with Pauli measurements, and guarantees robust determinism, however, it has been shown more recently that it fails to be a necessary condition. Our contribution is twofold. First, we demonstrate that Pauli flow is actually necessary for robust determinism in a weaker sense: given an open graph, i.e. a resource state, a deterministic computation can be driven iff it has a Pauli flow. However, the Pauli flows do not reflect all the possible correction strategies over a particular resource state, and properties like measurement order or computational depth are not necessarily reflected by a Pauli flow. Thus, to characterise determinism in full generality, we introduce a further extension called Shadow Pauli Flow that we prove necessary and sufficient for robust determinism: An MBQC is robustly deterministic if and only if its correction strategy is consistent with a Shadow Pauli flow. Furthermore, we show that Shadow Pauli flow can be computed in polynomial time.

.
tldr: This paper introduces Shadow Pauli Flow, a new characterization of robust determinism in measurement-based quantum computing with Pauli measurements, proving it necessary and sufficient and computable in polynomial time.
motivation: The existing Pauli Flow condition is not necessary for robust determinism in MBQC with Pauli measurements, leaving a gap in understanding when deterministic computation is possible. The authors aim to provide a complete characterization.
method: They define Shadow Pauli Flow, an extension of Pauli Flow, and prove that an MBQC is robustly deterministic if and only if its correction strategy is consistent with a Shadow Pauli flow. They also provide a polynomial-time algorithm to compute it.
result: Shadow Pauli Flow is both necessary and sufficient for robust determinism, and it can be computed in polynomial time, unlike previous conditions.
conclusion: This work provides a complete and efficient characterization of determinism in MBQC with Pauli measurements, advancing the theory of measurement-based quantum computing.

title: From Superradiance To Superabsorption: An Exact Treatment Of Non-Markovian Cooperative Radiation
authors: Ignacio González And Ángel Rivas
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2159 (2026).

We investigate the emergence of cooperative radiation phenomena in ensembles of two-level atoms coupled to a lossy resonant cavity beyond the Markovian and mean-field approximations. By deriving a complete analytical solution for the two-emitter case and employing a numerically exact method for larger ensembles, we characterize the full transition from Markovian to non-Markovian collective dynamics for systems of up to [MATH] emitters. Our results reveal three distinct regimes: a Markovian phase exhibiting the standard superradiant burst, a non-Markovian phase featuring spontaneous superabsorption of the emitted field, and a critical regime marked by pulsed collective emission. We show that the critical spectral width separating these behaviors increases monotonically with the number of emitters, demonstrating that environmental memory effects can be enhanced by cooperativity. Finally, we find that the superradiant scaling of the peak intensity progressively degrades with increasing system size, approaching a subquadratic law in the limit of a perfect cavity. In this regime, spontaneous superabsorption emerges as a distinct manifestation of non-Markovian cooperativity.

.
tldr: This paper provides an exact treatment of non-Markovian cooperative radiation in ensembles of two-level atoms coupled to a lossy cavity, revealing regimes of superradiance and superabsorption.
motivation: To understand cooperative radiation beyond Markovian and mean-field approximations, which is crucial for quantum technologies involving atom-cavity systems.
method: Derives an analytical solution for two emitters and uses a numerically exact method for larger ensembles, characterizing the transition from Markovian to non-Markovian dynamics.
result: Identifies three regimes: Markovian superradiant burst, non-Markovian superabsorption, and critical pulsed emission; shows that the critical spectral width increases with emitter number and that superradiant scaling degrades with system size.
conclusion: Environmental memory effects can be enhanced by cooperativity, and spontaneous superabsorption emerges as a distinct non-Markovian cooperative phenomenon.

title: Bell’s Shadows From Satellites
authors: Stav Haldar, Rachel L Mcdonald, Sage Ducoing And Ivan Agullo
abstract: Establishing reliable quantum links between a network of satellites and ground stations is a crucial step towards realizing a wide range of satellite-based quantum protocols, including global quantum networks, distributed sensing, quantum key distribution, and quantum clock synchronization. In this article, we envision a network of satellites and ground stations where quantum links are created through the exchange of entangled photon pairs. We simulate the dynamics of a satellite constellation and a set of Bell tests between the constellation and ground stations. We identify the regions on Earth where Bell tests can be successfully conducted with a satellite or a set of them, at a specified level of confidence. These regions move with the constellation and will be referred to as Bell violation shadows. We demonstrate that these shadows provide valuable insights for the study and evaluation of many satellite-mediated or satellite-assisted quantum protocols.
tldr: This paper simulates satellite constellations to identify moving regions on Earth where Bell tests can be successfully conducted, providing insights for satellite-based quantum protocols.
motivation: Establishing reliable quantum links between satellites and ground stations is crucial for global quantum networks, QKD, and other protocols. The authors aim to provide a tool for evaluating where and when Bell tests can be performed with satellite constellations.
method: They simulate the dynamics of a satellite constellation and ground stations, modeling the exchange of entangled photon pairs. They compute Bell violation shadows—regions on Earth where Bell tests can be conducted at a specified confidence level—and analyze their movement over time.
result: The simulations identify dynamic regions (shadows) where Bell tests are feasible, and demonstrate that these shadows can inform the design and evaluation of satellite-mediated quantum protocols.
conclusion: The concept of Bell violation shadows offers a valuable framework for planning and optimizing satellite-based quantum communication networks.

title: Promise Of Graph Sparsification And Decomposition For Noise Reduction In Qaoa: Analysis For Trapped-Ion Compilations
authors: Jai Moondra, Phillip C. Lotshaw, Greg Mohler, And Swati Gupta
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2185 (2026).

We develop new approximate compilation schemes that significantly reduce the expense of compiling the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for solving the Max-Cut problem. Our main focus is on compilation with trapped-ion simulators using Pauli-[MATH] operations and all-to-all Ising Hamiltonian [MATH] evolution generated by Molmer-Sorensen or optical dipole force interactions, though some of our results also apply to standard gate-based compilations. Our results are based on principles of graph sparsification and decomposition; the former reduces the number of edges in a graph while maintaining its cut structure, while the latter breaks a weighted graph into a small number of unweighted graphs. Though these techniques have been used as heuristics in various hybrid quantum algorithms, there have been no guarantees on their performance, to the best of our knowledge. This work provides the first provable guarantees using sparsification and decomposition to improve quantum noise resilience and reduce quantum circuit complexity. For quantum hardware that uses edge-by-edge QAOA compilations, sparsification leads to a direct reduction in circuit complexity. For trapped-ion quantum simulators implementing all-to-all [MATH] pulses, we show that for a [MATH] factor loss in the Max-Cut approximation ([MATH], our compilations improve the (worst-case) number of [MATH] pulses from [MATH] to [MATH] and the (worst-case) number of Pauli-[MATH] bit flips from [MATH] to [MATH] for [MATH]-node graphs. This is an asymptotic improvement for any constant [MATH]. We demonstrate that significant improvements to the approximation ratio are obtained using decomposition in simulated trapped-ion experiments with dephasing noise. We further present a generic argument showing that sparsification results in an exponentially improved circuit fidelity lower bound in digital computing schemes based on one- and two-qubit gates, which are relevant to a wide variety of hardwares such as superconducting qubits and certain neutral atom or trapped ion setups, and more sophisticated noise models. We anticipate these approximate compilation techniques will be useful tools in a variety of future quantum computing experiments.

.
tldr: This paper provides the first provable guarantees for using graph sparsification and decomposition to reduce circuit complexity and improve noise resilience in QAOA for Max-Cut, with specific improvements for trapped-ion compilations.
motivation: QAOA compilation for Max-Cut is expensive and noise-sensitive; graph sparsification and decomposition have been used heuristically but lack theoretical guarantees. The authors aim to provide provable improvements in circuit complexity and noise resilience.
method: They develop approximate compilation schemes based on graph sparsification (reducing edges while preserving cut structure) and decomposition (breaking weighted graphs into unweighted ones), and analyze their impact on circuit complexity and fidelity for trapped-ion and gate-based implementations.
result: For trapped-ion simulators, they achieve asymptotic improvements in the number of Molmer-Sorensen pulses and Pauli-X bit flips, and demonstrate improved approximation ratios under dephasing noise. They also show exponentially improved circuit fidelity lower bounds for digital schemes.
conclusion: These approximate compilation techniques offer practical benefits for near-term quantum computing, with provable guarantees that reduce circuit complexity and enhance noise resilience.

title: Entanglement Growth In The Dark Intervals Of A Locally Monitored Free-fermion Chain
authors: Giovanni Di Fresco, Youenn Le Gal, Davide Valenti, Marco Schiró, And Angelo Carollo
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2183 (2026).

We consider a free fermionic chain with monitoring of the particle density on a single site of the chain and study the entanglement dynamics of quantum jump trajectories. We show that the entanglement entropy grows in time towards a stationary state which display volume law scaling of the entropy, in stark contrast with both the unitary dynamics after a local quench and the no-click limit corresponding to full post-selection. We explain the extensive entanglement growth as a consequence of the peculiar distribution of quantum jumps in time, which display superpoissonian waiting time distribution characterised by a bunching of quantum jumps followed by long dark intervals where no-clicks are detected, akin to the distribution of fluorescence light in a driven atom. We show that the presence of dark intervals is the key feature to explain the effect and that by increasing the number of sites which are monitored the volume law scaling gives away to the Zeno effect and its associated area law.

.
tldr: This paper studies entanglement growth in a free-fermion chain under local monitoring, revealing volume-law scaling due to dark intervals in quantum jumps.
motivation: Understanding how measurement-induced dynamics affect entanglement in many-body systems is crucial for quantum information and thermodynamics.
method: The authors analyze quantum jump trajectories of a free-fermion chain with local density monitoring, deriving waiting time distributions and entanglement entropy scaling.
result: They find super-Poissonian waiting times with bunching and dark intervals, leading to volume-law entanglement, contrasting with unitary and no-click limits; increasing monitored sites induces Zeno effect and area law.
conclusion: Dark intervals in monitoring are key to extensive entanglement growth, offering insights into measurement-induced phases and quantum thermodynamics.

title: On The Quantum Computational Complexity Of Classical Linear Dynamics With Geometrically Local Interactions: Dequantization And Universality
authors: Kazuki Sakamoto And Keisuke Fujii
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2182 (2026).

The simulation of large-scale classical systems in exponentially small space on quantum computers has gained attention. The prior work demonstrated that a quantum algorithm offers an exponential speedup over any classical algorithm in simulating classical dynamics with long-range interactions. However, many real-world classical systems, such as those arising from partial differential equations, exhibit only local interactions. The question remains whether quantum algorithms can still provide exponential speedup under this condition. In this work, we thoroughly characterize the computational complexity of simulating such geometrically local systems on quantum computers. First, we dequantize the quantum algorithm for simulating short-time (polynomial-time) dynamics of such systems. This implies that the problem of simulating this dynamics does not yield any exponential quantum advantage. Second, we show that simulating short-time dynamics is at least as hard as polynomial-time and linear-space probabilistic classical computation. Third, we show that the computational complexity of simulating long-time (exponential-time) dynamics is captured by exponential-time and polynomial-space quantum computation. This suggests a super-polynomial time advantage when restricting the computation to polynomial-space, or an exponential space advantage otherwise. This work offers new insights into the complexity of classical dynamics governed by partial differential equations, providing a pathway for achieving quantum advantage in practical problems.

.
tldr: This paper characterizes the quantum computational complexity of simulating classical linear dynamics with geometrically local interactions, showing no exponential quantum advantage for short-time dynamics but potential super-polynomial advantage for long-time dynamics under space constraints.
motivation: To determine whether quantum computers can provide exponential speedup for simulating classical systems with local interactions, which are common in real-world applications like partial differential equations.
method: The authors dequantize the quantum algorithm for short-time dynamics, prove hardness results for short-time simulation, and analyze the complexity of long-time dynamics in terms of quantum complexity classes.
result: Short-time dynamics simulation is dequantized (no exponential advantage) and is as hard as polynomial-time linear-space probabilistic classical computation; long-time dynamics is captured by exponential-time polynomial-space quantum computation, suggesting super-polynomial time advantage under space restrictions.
conclusion: The work provides a thorough complexity characterization, indicating that quantum advantage for local classical dynamics may be limited to long-time simulations with space constraints, offering insights for practical quantum advantage.

title: Entanglement-assisted Quasi-cyclic Quantum Low-density Parity-check Codes Over Qubits
authors: Pavan Kumar, Abhi Kumar Sharma, Karthik Bharadwaj, And Shayan Srinivasa Garani
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2181 (2026).

We construct several families of entanglement-assisted quasi-cyclic quantum LDPC (EA-QC-QLDPC) codes via structured tilings of permutation matrices. The entanglement-unassisted portion of the joint Tanner graph of the proposed EA-QC-QLDPC code derived from two distinct classical QC-LDPC codes is free of 4-cycles. Notably, one of the proposed families constructed from two distinct classical codes requires only a [MATH] shared Bell pair between the quantum transmitter and receiver, highlighting its resource efficiency. We also analytically determine the exact code rates for some of the proposed constructions. Furthermore, two of the proposed families of EA-QC-QLDPC codes are derived from a single classical code whose Tanner graphs possess girth greater than six, further enhancing their error-correcting performance. We also propose an encoding scheme with improved complexity by exploiting the proposed code structure. The performance of the proposed codes is assessed under both random and burst error models under the depolarizing and Markovian noise actions. Simulation results reveal nearly one order of improvement in error-correction performance with the quaternary block-layered normalized min-sum (QBLNMS) decoder compared to the layered binary sum-product decoder over both depolarizing and Markovian channels. Using the QBLNMS decoder over a quaternary alphabet, we demonstrate that correlated Pauli errors can be effectively handled within the decoding framework. Furthermore, under the QBLNMS decoding, the proposed codes achieve [MATH] performance improvements compared to prior works and can effectively handle both random and burst errors. The code constructions are scalable across various coding rates and quantum payloads, crucial for practical quantum communication and computing systems.

.
tldr: This paper constructs entanglement-assisted quasi-cyclic quantum LDPC codes with improved error correction and resource efficiency.
motivation: Quantum error correction is essential for reliable quantum communication and computation, and constructing efficient quantum LDPC codes with good performance is a key challenge.
method: The authors construct EA-QC-QLDPC codes via structured tilings of permutation matrices, ensuring 4-cycle-free Tanner graphs and deriving exact rates for some families. They also propose an efficient encoding scheme and evaluate performance using QBLNMS and layered binary decoders.
result: The proposed codes show nearly an order of magnitude improvement in error-correction performance with QBLNMS decoder over depolarizing and Markovian channels, and require only one shared Bell pair for one family.
conclusion: The scalable constructions and improved decoding demonstrate practical potential for quantum communication and computing systems.

title: Atommovr: An Open-source Simulation Framework For Rearrangement In Atomic Arrays
authors: Nikhil K Harle, Bo-Yu Chen, Bob Bao, And Hannes Bernien
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2177 (2026).

The task of atom rearrangement has emerged in the last decade as a fundamental building block in the development of neutral atom-based quantum processors. As such processors grow to thousands of atoms, it becomes increasingly important to design algorithms robust to experimental sources of error. While recent progress has been made towards developing algorithms with favorable time scaling, such work has been limited to noiseless settings. Moreover, there is a lack of open-source code for reproducing and benchmarking existing algorithms. To address these deficiencies, we develop an open-source simulation framework, atommovr, and leverage it to study three distinct settings: 1) time-optimal, noiseless rearrangement, 2) noisy rearrangement under realistic error models, and 3) noiseless dual-species rearrangement. We extract lower bounds for time-optimal rearrangement, study advantageous strategies across different error regimes, and develop a novel dual-species algorithm, InsideOut, capable of avoiding 'blocked' configurations with a near-unity success rate. We hope that atommovr can serve as a common tool for the community to study rearrangement, lower the barrier to entry for new experimental groups, and stimulate progress in developing algorithms tailored to minimize atom loss in experiment.

.
tldr: This paper introduces an open-source simulation framework for atom rearrangement in neutral atom arrays, addressing time-optimal, noisy, and dual-species scenarios.
motivation: As neutral atom quantum processors scale to thousands of atoms, efficient and robust rearrangement algorithms are crucial, yet existing work lacks open-source tools and noise considerations.
method: The authors develop 'atommovr', a simulation framework, and use it to benchmark rearrangement algorithms under noiseless and noisy conditions, including a novel dual-species algorithm 'InsideOut'.
result: They extract lower bounds for time-optimal rearrangement, identify advantageous strategies across error regimes, and demonstrate that InsideOut avoids blocked configurations with near-unity success.
conclusion: The framework provides a common benchmarking tool for the community, lowering entry barriers and stimulating progress in atom rearrangement algorithms.

title: Pilot-Wave Simulator: Exact Classical Sampling From Ideal And Noisy Quantum Circuits Up To Hundreds Of Qubits
authors: Gleb Kalachev, Pavel Mosharev, Zuoheng Zou, Pavel Panteleev, And Man-Hong Yung
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2173 (2026).

Quantum circuit simulators running on classical computers offer a vital platform for designing, testing, and optimizing quantum algorithms, driving innovation despite limited access to real quantum hardware. However, their scalability is inherently constrained by exponential memory and computational overhead, which restricts accurate simulation of large-scale quantum circuits and often results in approximate output distributions. Here, we propose an exact sampling algorithm that integrates tensor network contraction techniques with a Markov process, wherein a classical state evolves according to the local structure of the quantum circuit. As a demonstration, we target the challenge of generating samples from ideal and noisy QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits, incorporating both depolarizing and amplitude damping noise models. These results enable further validation of several assumptions and conjectures at a scale previously out of reach, significantly expanding the scope of classical simulation in quantum algorithm research.

.
tldr: This paper presents an exact classical sampling algorithm for quantum circuits up to hundreds of qubits using tensor network contraction and Markov processes, demonstrated on QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits under noise.
motivation: Classical simulation of quantum circuits is crucial for validating quantum algorithms, but scalability is limited by exponential overhead. The authors aim to extend the reach of exact sampling to larger circuits, enabling tests of quantum advantage and noise models.
method: The algorithm integrates tensor network contraction with a Markov process, where a classical state evolves according to the local structure of the quantum circuit, allowing exact sampling from the output distribution.
result: They demonstrate exact sampling from ideal and noisy QAOA circuits with up to 476 qubits, incorporating depolarizing and amplitude damping noise, achieving a scale previously out of reach for exact simulation.
conclusion: This work significantly expands the scope of classical simulation in quantum algorithm research, providing a tool to validate assumptions and conjectures at larger scales, and may inform the study of quantum advantage.

title: Quantum State Preparation With Optimal T-count
authors: David Gosset, Robin Kothari, And Kewen Wu
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2168 (2026).

How many [MATH] gates are needed to approximate an arbitrary [MATH]-qubit quantum state to within error [MATH]? Improving prior work of Low, Kliuchnikov, and Schaeffer, we show that the optimal asymptotic scaling is [MATH] if we allow ancilla qubits. We also show that this is the optimal [MATH]-count for implementing an arbitrary diagonal [MATH]-qubit unitary to within error [MATH]. We describe applications in which a tensor product of many single-qubit unitaries can be synthesized in parallel for the price of one.

.
tldr: This paper determines the optimal T-count for quantum state preparation and diagonal unitary synthesis, showing that ancilla qubits enable asymptotically optimal scaling.
motivation: The number of T gates is a critical resource for fault-tolerant quantum computing, and prior work left gaps in the optimal scaling for state preparation and diagonal unitaries.
method: The authors provide constructive algorithms using ancilla qubits and prove matching lower bounds, improving on previous work by Low, Kliuchnikov, and Schaeffer.
result: They show that the optimal T-count for approximating an arbitrary n-qubit state to error epsilon is Theta(n^2 + log(1/epsilon)) with ancillas, and similarly for diagonal unitaries, with applications to parallel synthesis of tensor products of single-qubit unitaries.
conclusion: The results settle the optimal T-count for these tasks, offering practical improvements for quantum circuit synthesis and resource estimation.

title: Geometric Speed Limit Of State Preparation And Curved Control Spaces
authors: Maximilian Goll And Robert H. Jonsson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2160 (2026).

The preparation of quantum many-body systems faces the difficulty that in a realistic scenario only few control parameters of the system may be accessible. In this context, an interesting connection between the energy fluctuations during state preparation and its geometric length as measured by the Fubini-Study metric was discussed by Bukov et al. in 2019 [5]. An inspiring conjecture lower bounding the energy fluctuations by the minimal geometric length of all accessible state preparation protocols was put forward together with supporting examples and numerical evidence. However, we here show that the conjecture does not hold but can be violated if the accessible parameter space has extrinsic curvature, when embedded into the space of all dynamically accessible states. We illustrate this by a number of generic qubit, qutrit and harmonic oscillator systems.

.
tldr: This paper disproves a conjecture on geometric speed limits for state preparation by showing violations in systems with curved control spaces.
motivation: The authors aim to test a conjecture that energy fluctuations during state preparation are lower bounded by the minimal geometric length of accessible protocols, which would have implications for quantum control and thermodynamics.
method: They analyze qubit, qutrit, and harmonic oscillator systems, demonstrating that the conjecture fails when the accessible parameter space has extrinsic curvature.
result: They provide explicit counterexamples where the energy fluctuations are smaller than the conjectured bound, highlighting the role of curvature.
conclusion: The conjecture is not universally valid, and geometric speed limits must account for the curvature of the control space.

title: Near-Optimal Parameter Tuning Of Level-1 Qaoa For Ising Models
authors: V Vijendran, Dax Enshan Koh, Eunok Bae, Hyukjoon Kwon, Ping Koy Lam, And Syed M Assad
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2158 (2026).

The Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm (QAOA) tackles combinatorial optimisation problems by encoding their solutions into the ground state of an Ising Hamiltonian prepared by a [MATH]-level parameterised circuit, with the angles tuned classically. Parameter optimisation is widely regarded as a central bottleneck, even for the shallowest circuits. Focusing on QAOA at [MATH] (QAOA[MATH]), we show that tuning the two angles [MATH] for weighted Ising models is not a black-box search but a structured signal-processing problem. We prove that the QAOA[MATH] expectation value is a partial Fourier series in [MATH] whose frequencies are determined explicitly by the problem's couplings and fields, giving instance-wise bandwidth bounds and, via the Nyquist–Shannon theorem, the sampling resolution needed to avoid the aliasing that causes coarse-grid searches to return spurious optima. We then eliminate the mixer angle analytically, computing [MATH] in closed form to reduce the search to one dimension, and apply a subdivision algorithm that locates the globally optimal [MATH] in polynomial time with a certificate of optimality when the weights are commensurable and bounded. For regular weighted graphs, we further prove the conventional wisdom that the globally optimal [MATH] concentrates near zero and coincides with the first local optimum, giving a rigorous account of the empirical success of small-angle initialisation and allowing gradient descent to replace exhaustive line searches. Validated within Recursive QAOA (RQAOA) on weighted instances of 128 and 256 qubits, our method consistently outperforms both coarsely optimised RQAOA and semidefinite programming.

.
tldr: This paper provides a rigorous analysis of QAOA parameter optimization for Ising models, showing that the expectation value is a partial Fourier series and deriving optimal sampling and initialization strategies.
motivation: Parameter optimization is a central bottleneck in QAOA, and the authors aim to show that for level-1 QAOA on weighted Ising models, the problem is structured and can be solved efficiently.
method: The authors prove that the QAOA expectation value is a partial Fourier series with frequencies determined by the problem's couplings and fields, use the Nyquist-Shannon theorem to determine sampling resolution, eliminate the mixer angle analytically, and apply a subdivision algorithm for global optimization. They also prove concentration of the optimal angle near zero for regular graphs.
result: The method outperforms coarsely optimized RQAOA and semidefinite programming on weighted instances of 128 and 256 qubits, and provides certificates of optimality for commensurable weights.
conclusion: QAOA parameter tuning is not a black-box search but a structured signal-processing problem, enabling efficient and provably optimal optimization for level-1 QAOA.

title: Sparse Identification Of Quantum Hamiltonian Dynamics Via Quantum Circuit Learning
authors: Yusei Tateyama And Yuzuru Kato
abstract: Sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics (SINDy) is a data-driven framework for estimating classical nonlinear dynamical systems from time-series data. In this approach, system dynamics is represented as a linear combination of a predefined set of basis functions, and the corresponding coefficients are sparsely estimated from observed time-series data. In this study, we propose sparse identification of quantum Hamiltonian dynamics (SIQHDy), a SINDy-inspired quantum circuit learning framework for estimating quantum Hamiltonian dynamics from time-series data of quantum measurement outcomes. In SIQHDy, the unitary evolution of a quantum Hamiltonian system is expressed as a product of basis quantum circuits, and the corresponding circuit parameters are estimated through sparsity-promoting optimization. We numerically demonstrate that SIQHDy accurately reconstructs the dynamics of single-, three-, and five-spin systems, and exhibits robustness to measurement noise in the three-spin case. Furthermore, we propose an extension of SIQHDy for scenarios with limited accessible observables and evaluate its performance in identifying three-spin systems and in network-structure identification for five-spin systems.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum circuit learning framework inspired by SINDy to sparsely identify quantum Hamiltonian dynamics from measurement time-series data.
motivation: Estimating quantum Hamiltonian dynamics from data is crucial for characterizing quantum systems, but existing methods may require many measurements or lack interpretability. The authors aim to adapt classical sparse identification techniques to quantum systems.
method: The method, SIQHDy, represents the unitary evolution as a product of basis quantum circuits and estimates circuit parameters via sparsity-promoting optimization, with an extension for limited observables.
result: Numerical demonstrations show accurate reconstruction of single-, three-, and five-spin systems, robustness to noise in three-spin case, and successful network-structure identification for five-spin systems.
conclusion: SIQHDy provides a promising data-driven approach for identifying quantum Hamiltonians, potentially aiding in quantum system characterization and network inference.

title: Rotation-enhanced Photonic Spin Hall Effect In A Ring Bose–Einstein Condensate
authors: Leibo Deng, Muqaddar Abbas, Ghaisud Din, Hocine Bahlouli And Yong-Hong Ma
abstract: We show that rotation can strongly amplify the photonic spin Hall effect in a ring Bose–Einstein condensate. For an incident probe beam carrying orbital angular momentum (OAM), the spin-dependent transverse shift of the reflected light is weak in the non-rotating regime but becomes strongly enhanced under rotation because rotation lifts the degeneracy of the condensate mechanical modes via Bragg scattering. The resulting mode splitting produces large photonic spin Hall shifts at ultra-low optical power, with the enhancement increasing with both the condensate winding number and the probe OAM , while remaining weakly affected by atom–atom interactions. Our findings elucidate a rotation-governed mechanism underlying spin-dependent light transport in hybrid atom–optomechanical systems, thereby highlighting its potential for applications in high-precision rotational sensing.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that rotation can strongly enhance the photonic spin Hall effect in a ring Bose-Einstein condensate, enabling large spin-dependent shifts at ultra-low optical power.
motivation: The photonic spin Hall effect is typically weak, limiting its applications. The authors aim to find a mechanism to amplify this effect for high-precision sensing.
method: They theoretically analyze a ring Bose-Einstein condensate coupled to an optical cavity, considering the effects of rotation, orbital angular momentum of the probe beam, and atom-atom interactions on the spin-dependent transverse shift.
result: Rotation lifts the degeneracy of condensate mechanical modes via Bragg scattering, leading to mode splitting and a strongly enhanced photonic spin Hall shift. The enhancement increases with winding number and probe OAM, while being weakly affected by interactions.
